blocks.x: If there’s anything I know about Boston, it’s that this is a city that knows its seafood. Because of location and fishing heritage, we sling lobster rolls and oysters and fried clams by the bucket—so it should come as no surprise that sushi, too, has become a serious part of the city’s more upscale dining culture. Yes, travelers come here to experience our classic sea coast and clam shacks, but increasingly you’ll find that Boston has a robust enough sushi scene to excite international visitors, too—one that benefits not only from our abundant local fisheries, but also the international demand that make it possible to source special ingredients like fish flown in straight from Japan.

And closer look at Boston’s sushi restaurants of the past decade reveals the makings of a true scene; not only those destination, chef-driven restaurants worthy of special occasions, but also quieter neighborhood spots that Bostonians integrate into their regular takeout routines and locals line up for (Cafe Sushi, anyone?). And unlike lobster rolls, which have a pretty canonical form, sushi in Boston runs the gamut from highly traditional to the wildly inventive. If you’re coming to Boston, yes, seek out the fried clams and classics—but also make sure to pencil in some time for excellent sushi, too—including a newly minted Michelin-star spot. Here’s where.

blocks.x: If you want to understand why Boston’s sushi scene deserves to be taken seriously, start with O Ya. It’s set inside a century-old former firehouse in the Leather District, and it’s been one of the city’s most respectable reservations since it was opened by James Beard Award-winning chef Tim Cushman and his co-founder and wife Nancy Cushman in 2007. The heart of the experience is a 20-course omakase built around nigiri and sashimi, but “traditional sushi” this is not. Each bite is deliberately composed with the rhythm and crescendo of a piece of music, a reflection of Tim Cushman’s background as a musician, resulting in sushi that feels deeply considered but also playful. Don’t miss the sake program, one of the most robust in the country. O Ya turns 20 in 2027—and after two decades, it is still the sushi restaurant against which many of Boston’s newcomers are measured.

Great sushi doesn’t have to be precious, which is exactly what Cafe Sushi Shoten is selling. The longstanding Cambridge favorite evolved into a takeout-focused operation during the pandemic, but what some might see as a compromise has become part of its appeal. The sushi is meticulous, reliable, and remarkably fresh. You can pick up beautiful prepared bento boxes and signature rolls without committing to a three-hour omakase—making this a perfect regular spot for the neighborhood’s many locals and students.

Chef Gary Lei has a compelling story—he first came to the United States in 2010 and worked at the popular Sushi Den in Denver before moving to Boston, working at Uni for five years, and then starting his own operation in Cambridge in 2019. Rooted in tradition but unafraid to mix in new world creativity, he certainly has an eye for the theatrical. Garnishes are elaborate and creative—think bites of caviar-topped nigiri, duck breast arriving under a cloche, perhaps a little Japanese A5 wagyu as a decadent treat—but the details are highly precise, as well. An omakase menu spread over 18 courses, Umami lives up to its name with dishes that are deeply flavorful. Don’t miss the chance for sake pairings, which come in flexible options of three, four, or five glasses throughout your meal.
